title: Federated Authorization Access (4-party)
description: The resource has its own access server. The agent obtains a person token from its PS, presents it at the resource's authorization endpoint, and gets back a resource token whose aud is the AS URL. The PS federates with the AS — sending the resource token and the agent token — and the AS evaluates resource policy and issues the auth token. Only the PS may call the AS token endpoint, which is why a resource token issued to an agent that cannot name a person is one nobody can redeem.

events.label: Presented; its claims become the resource token's
Used to prove the agent's PS binding

steps.label: POST /person {resource} → 200 person_token
annotations: The agent signs with its agent token and names the resource it wants a person token for. resource is REQUIRED and becomes the token's aud.
The PS issues aa-person+jwt with a directed sub for that resource and cnf.jwk bound to the agent's signing key.
A person token carries no scope and no account — it identifies the person, it does not authorize anything.
The PS MAY require the person's approval first and return 202 with requirement=interaction.

steps.label: POST /authorize with the person token → 200 resource_token (aud=AS)
annotations: The agent presents the person token via Signature-Key. The resource MUST have verified one before it issues a resource token; without it the answer is 401 with requirement=person-token.
KEY DIFFERENCE from three-party: aud = the AS URL. The resource has its own access server and points the token at it.
ps, sub and presented_jti are copied out of the person token. The AS verifies only that ps names the PS that sent it the token request — resolving the person token itself is the PS's job.
agent_jkt binds the resource token to the agent's key. No agent identifier appears in it.
The same resource token also arrives on a 401 with requirement=auth-token when the agent calls an endpoint directly.

steps.label: POST resource token to PS → PS federates to AS → 200 + auth token
annotations: The agent POSTs the resource token to its PS's auth_token_endpoint (renamed from token_endpoint in -11), signing with its own agent token.
The PS resolves the person token named by presented_jti and verifies ps, sub, mission_s256 and tenant match it exactly before doing anything else.
aud is the AS, not the PS, so the PS federates on the agent's behalf (step 4 below).
In this autonomous flow the PS federates synchronously and returns the auth token directly.

steps.label: PS federates to AS /token
annotations: The PS posts the resource token and the agent token to the AS's auth_token_endpoint. This step is internal — the agent does not see it.
The PS signs with its own identity (sig=jwks_uri from its well-known metadata).
agent_token stays REQUIRED even though the resource never sees an agent identifier: the AS evaluates policy, and an agent token may carry attestation or workload claims that bear on it.
The AS verifies the resource token: iss=resource, aud=AS, ps names the PS that sent this request, agent_jkt matches the key the PS attests.
The resource token carries the person as ps and sub, so the AS needs no separate identity parameter.
The AS issues the auth token: iss=AS, dwk=aauth-access.json, aud=resource, ps=the person's PS, sub copied from the resource token, cnf.jwk=the agent's key. No agent identifier, no delegation chain.

steps.label: PS returns auth token to agent
annotations: The PS verifies the AS-issued auth token before handing it back to the agent.
The agent verifies iss matches the resource token's aud (the AS), aud matches the resource, cnf.jwk matches its own key, and sub matches the person token it presented to that resource.
The agent now holds a proof-of-possession auth token bound to its signing key.

steps.label: Retry with auth token → 200
annotations: The agent presents the AS-issued auth token in Signature-Key using sig=jwt, in place of the person token.
The resource verifies typ=aa-auth+jwt, discovers the AS's JWKS at {iss}/.well-known/aauth-access.json, checks aud is itself and cnf.jwk against the signing key.
It verifies sub is present and that (iss, sub) matches the record it established when it verified the person token.

interactive.description: Same 4-party flow, but the AS requires user consent before issuing the auth token. It returns 202 with a pending URL and an interaction URL. The agent polls while the user approves in a browser.

steps.label: POST resource token to PS → 202 (PS will federate to AS)

request_body.justification: Requesting read access to protected data

annotations: The agent POSTs the resource token to its PS's auth_token_endpoint.
The PS resolves the person token named by presented_jti and verifies its claims match before federating.
aud is the AS, so the PS federates — and the AS needs the person at its own interaction page, so the PS returns 202 with a pending URL and relays the AS's interaction requirement.

steps.label: PS federates to AS → AS returns 202 (interaction required)
annotations: The PS posts the resource token and the agent token to the AS's auth_token_endpoint. This step is internal — the agent does not see it.
The PS signs with its own identity (sig=jwks_uri from its well-known metadata).
agent_token stays REQUIRED even though the resource never sees an agent identifier: the AS evaluates policy, and an agent token may carry attestation or workload claims that bear on it.
The AS verifies the resource token: iss=resource, aud=AS, ps names the PS that sent this request, agent_jkt matches the key the PS attests.
The resource token carries the person as ps and sub, so the AS needs no separate identity parameter.
The AS cannot decide yet: it returns 202 with requirement=interaction and its own interaction URL.

steps.label: Poll PS pending URL → 202 (user has not approved yet)
annotations: Agent polls its PS's pending URL — not the AS directly.
PS is waiting for the user to approve at the AS. It returns 202 with status=pending.
Agent respects Retry-After and polls again later.

steps.label: User opens interaction URL → grants consent
steps.response_body:
Approve Agent Access

Agent: https://agent.example

Resource: https://api.example/data-auth

Scope: read write
annotations: AS renders a consent page summarizing the requesting agent, resource, and scope.
The user authenticates and approves the request in the browser.
Once approved, the pending request transitions to a token-ready state.

steps.label: Poll pending URL → 202 interacting
annotations: status=interacting: user has arrived at the consent page.
Agent stops prompting and keeps polling.
Next 200 delivers the auth token after user approves.

steps.label: Poll PS pending URL → 200 + auth token
annotations: User approved at the AS. The AS issued the auth token to the PS.
The PS's pending URL now returns 200 with the AS-issued auth token.
Agent verifies: iss=AS, aud=resource, cnf.jwk=its own key, act.sub=its own identifier.

steps.label: Retry with auth token → 200
annotations: Agent presents the AS-issued auth token in the Signature-Key header using sig=jwt.
Resource verifies: typ=aa-auth+jwt, iss=its own AS, aud=this resource, cnf.jwk matches signing key.
Resource also verifies act.sub matches the agent identifier.
Access granted. Full 4-party federation complete.

events.label: Presented; its claims become the resource token's
Used to prove the agent's PS binding
Interaction required
events.detail: PS federates to AS; AS requires user approval. PS returns 202 with its pending URL.

events.label: Polling — user not yet approved
events.detail: Agent polls PS pending URL. User has not yet visited the AS interaction page.

events.label: Poll — interacting
events.detail: User has arrived at the consent page; status=interacting. Agent stops prompting.

events.label: Approved
events.detail: User approved at AS. Agent polls PS and receives the AS-issued auth token.
